entities.name: Al Bu Said dynasty
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Al-Bu Said dynasty, founded 1744 in Oman by Ahmad ibn Said Al-Bu Said after driving out the Persian Afsharid occupation, is the ruling dynasty of the Sultanate of Oman — the oldest continuously ruling dynasty in the Arab world and one of the world's longest-reigning royal families. The dynasty established Oman as a major maritime empire in the 18th-19th centuries, controlling Zanzibar, the East African coast (Mombasa, Malindi), and trading posts in the Persian Gulf and India, making Muscat the dominant Indian Ocean commercial hub for a century.

Ahmad ibn Said's 1744 expulsion of Persian forces and election as Imam of Oman established the dynasty; his successors expanded maritime power dramatically. Sayyid Said bin Sultan (r. 1804-1856) moved the capital to Zanzibar in 1840, making it the center of the East African clove trade and the largest slave market in the Indian Ocean — Zanzibar exported 50,000-60,000 enslaved people annually at its peak. After Said's death, the empire split into Oman (under one son) and Zanzibar (under another), with Britain arbitrating the division in 1861.

Sultan Qaboos bin Said (r. 1970-2020) — who overthrew his isolationist father in a 1970 British-backed coup — transformed Oman from one of the world's most underdeveloped countries (only 3 schools, 10 km of paved roads in 1970) into a modern state using oil revenues, while maintaining Oman's tradition of balanced foreign policy ('Omani diplomacy') serving as mediator between the US and Iran. Qaboos's 50-year rule is considered the most successful modernization program in Gulf history.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The Al-Bu Said dynasty — ruling Oman for 280+ years as the Arab world's oldest continuous dynasty — achieved both the 19th century's most powerful Indian Ocean maritime empire (Zanzibar) and the 20th century's most dramatic Gulf modernization (Qaboos transforming 3-school Oman to modern state in 50 years).
